A watershed is the area of land that drains toward a common river, lake, or coastal inlet. Its boundaries follow the high ground separating neighboring drainage systems. Water falling on one side of a ridge may travel to a different ocean from water falling on the other side. Maps usually show the visible rivers, but a complete explanation must also account for water stored in soil, snow, vegetation, and underground rock.

After rainfall, some water runs directly across the surface. Another portion enters small spaces between soil particles. Plants draw on this stored moisture and release water vapor through their leaves. The amount that reaches a stream therefore depends on more than the amount of rain. Soil condition, slope, temperature, land cover, and earlier weather all influence the journey.

A navigator crossing an unfamiliar sea must answer two separate questions: where the vessel is now, and how to reach the intended destination. A compass helps with direction, but direction alone does not establish position. For centuries, sailors combined observations of the sky with estimates of speed, elapsed time, currents, and the shape of nearby coastlines. Each observation had limitations, so reliable navigation depended on comparing several kinds of evidence.

Latitude can be estimated from the height of a known celestial object above the horizon. Longitude presents a different problem because it depends on comparing local time with time at a reference location. Before accurate portable clocks became practical, a small timing error could translate into a substantial uncertainty in east-west position. Clouds and rough seas could make observations harder still.
